questions.problem: The function $v(t)=8{e}^{t/2}$ gives the volume, in cubic centimeters, of methylated spirit produced by a chemical process $t$ hours after the process begins. Find the instantaneous rate of change of spirit volume as a function of $t.$
questions.worked_solution:
The instantaneous rate of change of the spirit volume is equal to ${v}^{′}(t).$

Now, the rate of change of $v(t)$ with respect to $t$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(8{e}^{t/2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (8{e}^{t/2}) \\  & =4{e}^{t/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate change of the volume of spirit with respect to time is $4{e}^{t/2}$ cubic centimeters per hour.

questions.problem: The air temperature $F$ in degrees Fahrenheit can be modeled by the function $F(C)=\frac{9}{5}C+32,$ where $C$ is the air temperature in degrees Celsius. Find the instantaneous rate of change of the air temperature in degrees Fahrenheit with respect to the air temperature in degrees Celsius.
questions.worked_solution:
The instantaneous rate of change of the air temperature in degrees Fahrenheit with respect to the air temperature in degrees Celsius is equal to ${F}^{′}(C).$

Now, the rate of change of $F(C)$ with respect to $C$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(C) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}C}(\frac{9}{5}C+32) \\  & =\frac{9}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate change of the air temperature in degrees Fahrenheit with respect to the air temperature in degrees Celsius is $\frac{9}{5}$ degrees Fahrenheit per degree of Celsius.

questions.problem:
The funding $F,$ in millions of dollars, allocated to a research project $t$ years after it begins is modeled by

$$
F(t)=5+(t+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1),\,t\ge 0.
$$

What is the instantaneous rate of change of the funding as a function of $t?$

The instantaneous rate of change of the funding is
{{field-1}} million dollars per year.
questions.worked_solution:
The instantaneous rate of change of the funding is ${F}^{′}(t).$

We take the derivative and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =\frac{d}{dt}[5+(t+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)] \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)+(t+1)\cdot \frac{1}{t+1} \\  & =1+\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate of change of the funding is $1+\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)$ million dollars per year.

questions.problem:
The inventory level $I,$ in hundreds of units, of a medical supply $t$ weeks after ordering begins, is modeled by

$$
I(t)={t}^{2}{e}^{-t}+12,\,t\ge 0.
$$

What is the instantaneous rate of change of the inventory level as a function of $t?$ 

The instantaneous rate of change of the inventory level is
{{field-1}} hundreds of units per week.
questions.worked_solution:
The instantaneous rate of change of the inventory level is ${I}^{′}(t).$

We take the derivative and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}^{′}(t) & =\frac{d}{dt}[{t}^{2}{e}^{-t}+12] \\  & =2t{e}^{-t}+{t}^{2}\cdot (-{e}^{-t}) \\  & =2t{e}^{-t}-{t}^{2}{e}^{-t} \\  & =t{e}^{-t}(2-t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate of change of the inventory level is $t{e}^{-t}(2-t)$ hundreds of units per week.

questions.problem: The function $P(t)=710\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{e}^{t})$ represents the volume of milk, in liters, produced on a farm $t$ days after the owner bought new cows. What is the instantaneous rate of change of the volume of produced milk as a function of $t?$
questions.worked_solution:
The instantaneous rate of change of the volume of produced milk with respect to time is ${P}^{′}(t).$

Now, the rate of change of $P(t)$ with respect to $t$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(710\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+{e}^{t})) \\  & =710\,\frac{{e}^{t}}{1+{e}^{t}} \\  & =\frac{710}{1+{e}^{-t}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate of change of the volume of produced milk is  $\frac{710}{1+{e}^{-t}}$ liters per day.

questions.knowledge_point: Determining a Rate of Change for a Given Function at a Point
questions.problem: The temperature, in degrees Fahrenheit, of a rapidly cooling substance after $t$ minutes can be modeled by the function $F(t)=250-{t}^{3}.$ Find the instantaneous rate at which the temperature of the substance is changing with respect to time at the moment when the temperature of the substance is equal to $34$ degrees Fahrenheit.
questions.worked_solution:
Since we are given that the temperature of the substance is $34$ degrees Fahrenheit, the time can be calculated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}34 & =250-{t}^{3} \\ {t}^{3} & =216 \\ t & =6\end{aligned}
$$

The instantaneous rate at which the temperature of the substance is changing when $t=6$ minutes is equal to ${F}^{′}(6).$

Taking the derivative, the rate of change of $F(t)$ with respect to $t$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(250-{t}^{3})=-3{t}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

and evaluating at $t=6$ gives

$$
{F}^{′}(6)=-3(6)^{2}=-108.
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate at which the temperature of the substance is changing when $t=6$ minutes is $-108$ degrees Fahrenheit per minute.

questions.knowledge_point: Determining a Rate of Change for a Given Function at a Point
questions.problem: The number of computers affected by the spread of some ransomware after $t$ days can be modeled by the function $f(t)=\frac{100\,({t}^{3}+2)}{t+1}.$ What is the instantaneous rate of change in the number of infected computers when $t=9$ days?
questions.worked_solution:
The instantaneous rate of change in the spread when $t=9$ days is equal to ${f}^{′}(9).$ 

First, we take the derivative and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{100\,({t}^{3}+2)}{t+1}) \\  & =\frac{100(3{t}^{2})(t+1)-100({t}^{3}+2)(1)}{{(t+1)}^{2}} \\  & =100\cdot \frac{2{t}^{3}+3{t}^{2}-2}{{(t+1)}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $t=9,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(9) & =100\cdot \frac{2(9)^{3}+3(9)^{2}-2}{{((9)+1)}^{2}} \\  & =100\cdot \frac{1\,458+243-2}{100} \\  & =1\,699.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate of change in the spread when $t=9$ is $1\,699$ computers per day.

questions.knowledge_point: Determining a Rate of Change for a Given Function at a Point
questions.problem:
The concentration $C$ (in millimoles per liter) of a chemical in a reactor $t$ minutes after the reaction begins is modeled by the function $C(t)={t}^{3}+25$ for $0\le t\le 10.$ Find the instantaneous rate at which the concentration is changing with respect to time at the moment when the concentration is $150$ millimoles per liter.

The instantaneous rate of change when the concentration is $150$ millimoles per liter is
{{field-1}} millimoles per liter per minute.
questions.worked_solution:
Since we are given that the chemical's concentration is $150$ millimoles per liter, the time can be calculated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}C(t) & =150 \\ {t}^{3}+25 & =150 \\ {t}^{3} & =125 \\ t & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

The instantaneous rate at which the chemical's concentration is changing when $t=5$ minutes is equal to ${C}^{′}(5).$

Taking the derivative, the rate of change of $C(t)$ with respect to $t$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}+25) \\  & =3{t}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

and evaluating at $t=5$ gives

$$
{C}^{′}(5)=3(5)^{2}=75.
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate of change of the chemical's concentration when its concentration is $150$ millimoles per liter is  $75$ millimoles per liter per minute.

questions.problem: The function $g(p)={e}^{-4{p}^{2}}$ models the volume of gas that a vendor can sell, in liters, at a price of $p$ dollars per liter. Find the instantaneous rate at which the volume of gas is changing with respect to the price when $p=1.50$ dollars.
questions.worked_solution:
The instantaneous rate at which the volume of gas that can be sold is changing when $p=1.50$ dollars is equal to ${g}^{′}(1.5).$

Taking the derivative, the rate of change of $g(p)$ with respect to $p$ is 

$$
{g}^{′}(p)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}p}({e}^{-4{p}^{2}})=-8p{e}^{-4{p}^{2}},
$$

and evaluating at $p=1.5$ gives

$$
{g}^{′}(1.5)=-8(1.5){e}^{-4(1.5)^{2}}=-12{e}^{-9}.
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate at which the volume of gas that can be sold is changing when $p=1.5$ dollars is $-12{e}^{-9}$ liters per dollar.

questions.problem: The function $x(t)={t}^{2}+t$ models the distance traveled by a car $t$ seconds after it sets off on a journey. Find the instantaneous rate at which the distance traveled by the car is changing with respect to time when $t=1$ second.
questions.worked_solution:
The instantaneous rate at which the distance traveled by the car is changing when $t=1$ second is equal to ${x}^{′}(1).$

Taking the derivative, the rate of change of $x(t)$ with respect to $t$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{2}+t)=2t+1,\end{aligned}
$$

and evaluating at $t=1$ gives

$$
{x}^{′}(1)=2(1)+1=3.
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate at which the distance traveled by the car is changing when $t=1$ second is $3$ meters per second.

questions.knowledge_point: Further Determining Rates of Change in Geometrical Settings
questions.problem:
The surface area $A$ of a sphere is increasing. Find the instantaneous rate at which the surface area of the sphere is changing with respect to its radius at the moment when the radius of the sphere is equal to $5\,\text{in}.$

The instantaneous rate of change at the moment when its radius is $5$ inches is equal to
{{field-1}} ${\text{in}}^{2}/\text{in}.$
questions.worked_solution:
We know that the surface area of a sphere with radius $r$ is given by 

$$
A=A(r)=4\pi {r}^{2}.
$$

Taking the derivative, the rate of change of $A(r)$ with respect to $r$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(r) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(4\pi {r}^{2}) \\  & =4\pi (2r) \\  & =8\pi r,\end{aligned}
$$

and evaluating at $r=5$ gives

$$
{A}^{′}(5)=8\pi (5)=40\pi .
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate at which the surface area of the sphere is changing when its radius is $5\,\text{in}$, is $40\pi $ ${\text{in}}^{2}/\text{in}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14037675/assets/f59f65e184ccf4fdf2ae2124543ece45d41afce09d743dec9f17730dd00124d4.png)

The area $A$ of the circle above is increasing. The circumference and radius of the circle are $C$ and $r$ respectively. 
Find the rate of change of the area of the circle with respect to its circumference.
questions.worked_solution:
The area of a circle is given by

$$
A=\pi {r}^{2},
$$

where $r$ is the radius of the circle.

We know that $C=2\pi r.$ so we can express the area $A$ as a function of the circumference $C$ by substituting $r=\frac{C}{2\pi }$ in the formula above. We get

$$
A=\pi {r}^{2}=\pi {(\frac{C}{2\pi })}^{2}=\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }.
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $A(C)$ with respect to $C$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(C) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}C}(\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }) \\  & =\frac{1}{4\pi }\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}C}({C}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4\pi }(2C) \\  & =\frac{C}{2\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

The volume of a cube-shaped container is increasing. Find the instantaneous rate at which the volume of the container is changing with respect to the side length at the moment when the face diagonal of the cube is equal to $10\sqrt{2}\,\text{cm}.$

The instantaneous rate of change at the moment when the face diagonal is $10\sqrt{2}$ centimeters is equal to
{{field-1}} ${\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{cm}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since we are given that the face diagonal of the cube is $10\sqrt{2}\,\text{cm}$, its side length $s$ is $10\,\text{cm}.$ Now, the volume of a cube with side length $s$ is given by 

$$
V=V(s)={s}^{3}.
$$

Taking the derivative, the rate of change of $V(s)$ with respect to $s$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}^{′}(s) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}({s}^{3}) \\  & =3{s}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

and evaluating at $s=10$ gives

$$
{V}^{′}(10)=3(10)^{2}=300.
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate at which the volume of the container is increasing when the face diagonal is $10\sqrt{2}\,\text{cm}$ is $300\,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{cm}.$

questions.problem:
The volume of a right square pyramid is increasing. Given that its height $h$ is always twice the length of a base, find the rate of change of the volume of the pyramid with respect to its base length $s.$

*Hint*: The volume of a right square pyramid is $V=\frac{1}{3}{s}^{2}h.$ 

The rate of change of the pyramid’s volume with respect to $s$ is 
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We are given that $h=2s,$ so we can express the volume of the pyramid $V$ as a function of the base edge length $s$ by substituting $h=2s$ in the formula of the volume. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}V(s) & =\frac{1}{3}{s}^{2}h \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{s}^{2}(2s) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}{s}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the rate of change of $V(s)$ with respect to $s$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}^{′}(s) & =\frac{d}{ds}\,(\frac{2}{3}{s}^{3}) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\cdot \frac{d}{ds}\,({s}^{3}) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\cdot 3{s}^{2} \\  & =2{s}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, the rate of change of the pyramid’s volume with respect to its base length $s$ is $2{s}^{2}.$

A spherical balloon is being inflated so that its volume is increasing. Find the instantaneous rate at which the volume of the balloon is changing with respect to the radius at the moment when the diameter of the balloon is equal to $20\,\text{cm}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since we are given that the diameter of the spherical balloon is $20\,\text{cm}$,  its radius $r$ is $10\,\text{cm}.$ Now, the volume of a sphere with radius $r$  is given by 

$$
V=V(r)=\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}.
$$

Taking the derivative, the rate of change of $V(r)$ with respect to $r$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{V}^{′}(r) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\pi (3{r}^{2}) \\  & =4\pi {r}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

and evaluating at $r=10$ gives

$$
{V}^{′}(10)=4\pi (10)^{2}=400\pi .
$$

Therefore,  the instantaneous rate at which the volume of the balloon is increasing when the diameter is $20\,\text{cm}$ is $400\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{cm}.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Determining a Rate of Change for a Given Function
canonical_examples.problem: A particle moves in a straight line. After $t$ seconds the particle is $\, f(t)=2t^3 - 5t + 9\,$ feet away from its initial position. What is the instantaneous rate of change of the particle's position as a function of $t?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The instantaneous rate of change of the particle's position is equal to $f'(t).$ 

We take the derivative and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{3}-5t+9) \\  & =6{t}^{2}-5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, after $t$ seconds, the instantaneous rate of change of the particle's position is $6t^2 - 5$ feet per second.

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Determining a Rate of Change for a Given Function at a Point
canonical_examples.problem: Lizzie buys $b$ pounds of bananas at a price $p,$ in dollars, that can be modeled by the function $p(b)=5e^{-0.2b}.$ What is the instantaneous rate of change of the price when $b=5$ pounds?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The instantaneous rate of change of the price when $b=5$ pounds is equal to $p'(5).$

First, we take the derivative and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{p}^{′}(b) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}b}(5{e}^{-0.2b}) \\  & =5{e}^{-0.2b}\cdot (-0.2) \\  & =-{e}^{-0.2b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $b=5,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{p}^{′}(5) & =-{e}^{-0.2(5)} \\  & =-{e}^{-1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{e}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate change of the price when $b=5$ pounds is $-\dfrac{1}{e}$ dollars per pound.

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Further Determining Rates of Change in Geometrical Settings
canonical_examples.problem:
A spherical balloon is being inflated so that its volume is increasing. Find the instantaneous rate at which the volume of the balloon is changing with respect to the radius at the moment when the diameter of the balloon is equal to $12\, \text{cm}.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14037675/assets/e03fb046f74771676d7b1e83a1cf09176adcffaf8112e9de263404b8be74b026.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since we are given that the diameter of the balloon is $12\, \text{cm},$ its radius is $r =6\, \text{cm}.$ Now, we know that the volume of a sphere with radius $r$  is given by 

$$
V= V(r) = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3.
$$

Taking the derivative, the rate of change of $V(r)$  with respect to $r$ is 

$$
\eqalign{

V'(r) &= \dfrac{\textrm d }{\textrm d r}\left(  \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3\right)\[5pt]
 &  =  \dfrac{4}{3}\pi (3r^2)\[5pt]
 &= 4\pi r^2, 
}
$$

and evaluating at $r=6$ gives

$$
V'(6)=  4\pi (6)^2= 144\pi.
$$

Therefore, the instantaneous rate at which the volume of the balloon is changing when its diameter is $12\, \text{cm}\,$ is $\, 144\pi \, \text{cm}^3/\text{cm}.$

**Note:** We read $\text{cm}^3/\text{cm}$ as "centimeters cubed per centimeter".
